# Exact finite-knot replacement of inverse arms

This note proves a finite-dimensional reduction for a finite list of cap slopes in the horizontal-tangent homothetic-profile problem. It does not prove the required cap inequality. There is no assumption that a global constrained profile extremizer has qualified multipliers. Instead, local replacement preserves all the actual cap, section, and moment records exactly.

The only contact-theorem dependency is the proved lemma in `candidate bd886f63d6450164`, independently audited in `unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)`. Its statement is recalled here: if A is concave on an open interval, w>0, H has one sign, H''=w(av+b+cA), and supp(-A'') is contained in {H=0}, then the curvature has at most two support points when c is nonzero or when c=0 and av+b is nonzero. The case of identically zero coefficient data is excluded from that lemma. All applications below have nonzero coefficient data, and the needed duals are proved to exist. The expression av+b+cA may vanish identically when c is nonzero; it then forces A to be affine and causes no exception.

## 1. Ordinary curvature on a closed internal cell

Let I=[a,b], a<b, and let w be continuous and nonnegative on I, strictly positive on its interior. Let A be continuous, nonnegative, concave, and nonincreasing on I. Suppose its two inward endpoint slopes

    sL=A'_+(a),   sR=A'_-(b)

are finite. In particular sL>=sR and sL<=0. There is a continuous, nonnegative, concave, nonincreasing piecewise affine replacement Ahat with the same endpoint values, with join slopes no larger than sL at the left and no smaller than sR at the right, and with

    int_I w Ahat = int_I w A,
    int_I v w Ahat = int_I v w A,
    int_I w Ahat^2 = int_I w A^2.                    (1)

Its curvature on the closed cell uses at most eight atoms. Endpoint atoms are allowed: they mean that its internal slope can drop at a or that its slope can rise when viewed from the interior toward b. When this replacement is inserted between the original outside pieces, the actual slope across each join still decreases, so the resulting global arm is concave.

Here and below an endpoint curvature atom is bookkeeping for such a join; the function value itself does not jump.

### Proof of existence and the eight-atom bound

Write mu=-A'' on (a,b). Its mass is N=sL-sR. If N=0, A is already affine. Otherwise N>0, and

    A(v)=A(a)+sL(v-a)-int_(a,b) (v-t)_+ dmu(t).     (2)

Allow replacement measures on the CLOSED interval I. Keep their mass N and first moment int t dmu fixed. The first moment fixes A(b), while the mass fixes the slope after the cell. Every such nonnegative measure defines a concave arm by (2). Its initial internal slope is at most sL; every subsequent slope is no larger. Its final internal slope is sR plus its possible atom at b, hence is at least sR and at most sL. The function has the original two endpoint values, so nonnegativity follows from concavity.

Define

    T0(t)=int_t^b (v-t)w(v)dv,
    T1(t)=int_t^b (v-t)v w(v)dv.                    (3)

By Fubini, fixing int T0 dmu and int T1 dmu fixes the first two integrals in (1). Thus the feasible curvature measures have four linear records: mass, first moment, and the two T moments. They form a nonempty compact convex set in the weak topology. Compactness is the ordinary compactness of bounded nonnegative measures on a compact interval; each of the four kernels is continuous.

The map mu -> A_mu is continuous into L2(w dv): at each v the kernel (v-t)_+ is continuous and bounded in t, and dominated convergence then gives L2 convergence. This map is injective among measures with fixed mass. Equality of the arms recovers the curvature on [a,b), including the left-endpoint atom; the mass then recovers the atom at b. Consequently

    J(mu)=int_I w A_mu^2

is strictly convex on this fixed-mass class and continuous. It has a minimum and a maximum in the four-record feasible set.

Every maximum is an extreme point. Otherwise it would be the midpoint of two distinct feasible measures, and strict convexity would make its J value strictly smaller than the average of theirs. An extreme point has at most four support points: if it had five, choose five disjoint Borel sets of positive measure and a nonzero linear dependence among their four record vectors. A sufficiently small signed perturbation, constant relative to mu on each selected set, preserves all four records and keeps both signs of the perturbation nonnegative. This contradicts extremality. Hence a maximizing curvature measure uses at most four atoms.

We now prove that some minimizing measure also uses at most four atoms, without a constraint qualification assumption. Normalize mass to N and consider the moment curve

    t -> (t,T0(t),T1(t)) in R^3.

Its affine span is all of R^3. Indeed if c0+c1 t+c2 T0+c3 T1 is identically zero, differentiating twice in the interior gives w(t)(c2+c3 t)=0. Thus c2=c3=0, and then c0=c1=0.

Let q be the prescribed normalized moment vector. If q is on the boundary of the convex hull of this curve, a supporting affine function gives a nonzero continuous function

    H(t)=c0+c1 t+c2 T0(t)+c3 T1(t)>=0,
    supp(mu) subset {H=0}                         (4)

for EVERY feasible mu. If c2=c3=0, this nonzero affine function has at most one zero on I. Otherwise H''=w(c2+c3 t) has a nonzero affine load, so the contact lemma bounds the interior curvature support by two points. Together with the two endpoints this gives at most four support points.

If q is in the interior, define F(q') as the minimum of J over measures with normalized moment vector q'. The function F is finite and convex on the moment hull: convex combinations of measures have the interpolated moments, and J is convex. Its epigraph is closed by compactness. A supporting hyperplane at (q,F(q)) has a nonzero coefficient of the value coordinate, because q is interior; a purely horizontal supporting hyperplane would support the moment hull at an interior point. Normalizing this coefficient gives a vector lambda with

    F(q') >= F(q)+lambda.(q'-q).

This is a normal multiplier for a CONVEX problem with linear moments, not a multiplier for the original quadratic equality problem.

A minimizing mu therefore minimizes J minus a linear combination of its three moments among all measures of mass N. Its first variation against a point mass, and then against all probability measures, gives a continuous nonnegative function H, zero on supp(mu), of the form

    H(t)=-2 int_t^b (v-t)w(v)A_mu(v)dv
          -lambda1 t-lambda2 T0(t)-lambda3 T1(t)-c.

The harmless scaling of lambda by N has been absorbed into its notation. Consequently

    H''(t)=w(t)[-2A_mu(t)-lambda2-lambda3 t].       (5)

Its arm coefficient is -2, so the contact lemma applies without a zero-load exception. It gives at most two interior curvature atoms, plus the two endpoints. This proves the claimed four-atom minimizing representative.

Let mu_min and mu_max be such minimizers and maximizers. Their convex combinations retain all four linear records. The quadratic integral varies continuously between its minimum and maximum, so the intermediate value theorem gives a combination with exactly the original value J(mu). Its support is contained in the union of two sets of at most four points. Formula (2) gives Ahat and proves (1). No monotonicity of the quadratic integral along that segment is required. QED.

## 2. The terminal cell, including an infinite terminal slope

Let I=[a,R]. Assume the same conditions on w and A, but require only the finite initial slope sL=A'_+(a). No finite derivative at R is assumed. There is a replacement Ahat, piecewise affine with at most seven curvature atoms in the terminal representation, preserving all three integrals (1), preserving A(a), satisfying

    Ahat(R)>=A(R),

and remaining nonnegative, nonincreasing, and concave. Its initial internal slope is at most sL. Raising the terminal value is permitted ONLY at the global top level R; it would not preserve a fixed internal interpolation value.

### Weighted curvature and compactness

For v<R the ordinary representation is

    A(v)=A(a)+sL(v-a)-int_(a,v) (v-t) dmu(t),

where mu=-A''. Monotone convergence at R shows that the weighted measure

    dnu(t)=(R-t)dmu(t)

has finite mass

    N=A(a)+sL(R-a)-A(R)>=0.                       (6)

If N=0, A is affine. Otherwise allow measures nu of mass N on the CLOSED interval [a,R], and set, for v<R,

    A_nu(v)=A(a)+sL(v-a)-int k(v,t)dnu(t),
    k(v,t)=(v-t)_+/(R-t) for t<R,
    k(v,R)=0.                                    (7)

The value at R is always the upper-semicontinuous completion, namely the left limit. Thus

    A_nu(R)=A(R)+nu{R}.                           (8)

The atom at R is invisible to the interior arm and to every integral record. It is slack recording precisely the possible increase in the completed top value; it is not an actual jump of the completed arm.

Every arm in (7) is nonincreasing and concave. Its completed endpoint is nonnegative by (8), hence the entire arm is nonnegative. A weakly convergent sequence nu_j gives pointwise convergence for every v<R because k(v,.) is continuous, including at t=R. Since 0<=k<=1, it also gives L2(w dv) convergence. Equivalently, the L2 norm of the kernel tends to zero when its curvature location tends to R. This is why an infinite original terminal slope causes no failure of compactness.

Keep the two linear records

    int K0(t)dnu(t),  int K1(t)dnu(t),
    Ki(t)=Ti(t)/(R-t) for t<R,  Ki(R)=0,           (9)

where Ti are as in (3), with b=R. They preserve int wA and int vwA. The Ki are continuous on the closed cell. Their normalized moment curve (K0,K1) has full affine span in R^2: a relation c0+c1K0+c2K1=0 first gives c0=0 by evaluation at R; multiplying by R-t and differentiating twice then gives w(t)(c1+c2t)=0.

The same min/max argument now applies to a compact convex set with THREE linear records, namely mass and the two K moments. The fixed-mass map nu -> A_nu in L2 is injective: equal arms recover nu on [a,R), and fixed total mass recovers its atom at R. Therefore the quadratic maximum is attained at an extreme measure with at most three atoms.

For the minimum, boundary moment data give a nonzero function W=c0+c1K0+c2K1>=0 with support contained in its zeros. Multiply it by R-t and call the product H. On the interior,

    H''=w(c1+c2t).

The affine load is nonzero: otherwise W would be a nonzero constant, which cannot vanish on a positive-mass feasible measure. The contact lemma bounds interior support by two points; the endpoints add at most two.

For interior moment data, the convex value function again has a normal supporting plane. The first variation of the quadratic minimum gives W>=0, zero on support. After multiplication by R-t its second derivative is

    H''=w[-2A_nu-lambda0-lambda1 t].              (10)

The curvature of A_nu on the open interval is nu/(R-t), so the support condition is exactly the one required in the contact lemma. The coefficient -2 is nonzero. Thus a minimizing measure has at most four atoms including the endpoints.

Interpolating this four-atom minimum with the three-atom maximum matches the original quadratic integral and uses at most seven atoms. An atom at R may then be discarded from the representation: it already contributes zero to (7), and (8) gives the completed endpoint. All integral records remain exact. QED.

## 3. Global assembly without changing any finite cap record

Fix d=m+1>=2 and R>0. Let A_+,A_- be inverse arms of a concave homothetic profile whose maximum R occurs at the source zero. They are continuous, nonnegative, nonincreasing, and concave on [0,R], and A_+(0),A_-(0)>0. A positive top value records a plateau and is allowed. Fix finitely many positive slopes s_1,...,s_q, and let a_(epsilon,j) be the intersection level on arm epsilon:

    a_(epsilon,j)=max{v:A_epsilon(v)>=s_j v}.

These levels are positive. At a level less than R there is equality A(a)=s_j a; at R only A(R)>=s_jR is required.

For each arm separately, partition [0,R] at its distinct internal intersection levels. On each nonterminal cell use Section 1, with the original finite inward slopes. On the terminal cell use Section 2. All slopes at internal grid points are finite because the original arm is finite concave on a neighborhood of that point. The initial right slope at zero is also finite: a finite nonincreasing concave function has a nonpositive initial derivative bounded below by any subsequent chord slope.

For m>=2 use w(v)=v^(m-2). It is continuous and positive on every cell interior, even when a cell starts at zero. For m=1 use the artificial weight w=1. Matching the extra moments in that case is harmless and avoids any v^-1 weight.

Each internal replacement keeps its grid endpoint values. Its internal left slope is no greater than the old right slope, and its internal right slope is no less than the old left slope. At a shared grid point, therefore,

    new left slope >= old left slope
                   >= old right slope >= new right slope.

Thus the assembled arm is globally concave. It is nonincreasing on every cell and continuous at the joins. The last endpoint may rise, but the arm there is its continuous completed piecewise affine function; concavity and nonnegativity remain valid. Existing curvature atoms at grid points are retained as part of the joins, with any new endpoint atoms simply adding nonnegative slope drops.

Every internal intersection level is unchanged because its value is unchanged and A(v)-s_jv is strictly decreasing. A top-saturated level R remains top-saturated because the top value can only increase. A cellwise bound of eight new curvature atoms, together with the grid points, gives, conservatively, at most 9(q+1) curvature locations per arm. No significance is attached to this nonoptimal numerical bound.

For m>=2, the three moments preserved on every cell are

    int v^(m-2)A,
    int v^(m-1)A,
    int v^(m-2)A^2.                              (11)

They preserve the following records at EVERY selected positive slope, not merely their centered mixtures:

    C_s(A)=a_s^m/2
         +(m-1)/(2s) int_(a_s)^R v^(m-2)A(v)dv,

    K_s(A)=s a_s^(m+1)/4
         +(m-1)/(4s) int_(a_s)^R v^(m-2)A(v)^2dv,

    J_s(A)=(m/2)int_0^(a_s)v^(m-1)A(v)dv
         -s a_s^(m+1)/4
         +(m-1)/(4s)int_(a_s)^R v^(m-2)A(v)^2dv.

They also preserve the individual arm volume

    V_arm=m int_0^R v^(m-1)A(v)dv.

For m=1 all terms with m-1 are absent. The fixed intersections and the preserved integrals int A on every cell preserve exactly the same records. At s=0 use the separate one-arm formulas C_0(A)=R^m/2, K_0(A)=0, J_0(A)=V_arm/2. The total coarea is C(0)=R^m. No expression involving 1/s is used.

Consequently the total V, each C(s), each M(s)=K_s(A_+)-K_s(A_-), and each cap mass P(s)=V/2+J_s(A_+)-J_s(A_-) are unchanged. Every finite same-orientation centering constraint and every finite interval-overlap test based on these records is preserved exactly.

## 4. Reconstruction and precise scope

The replaced arms define the closed hypograph

    { (z,v): 0<=v<=R, -Ahat_-(v)<=z<=Ahat_+(v) }.

It is convex: its left boundary is convex in v and its right boundary is concave. Its upper boundary is therefore a concave profile rhat(z). Because the two arm values at zero remain positive and concavity gives Ahat(v)>=Ahat(0)(1-v/R), the source zero remains interior to the profile domain, with maximum height R. Finite piecewise affine arms give a finite piecewise affine profile; horizontal arm pieces become vertical endpoint faces, and positive top values become a central top plateau.

The replacement may remove an original initial flat arm segment. Thus the new profile may have height zero at an outer endpoint even when the original profile was positive on its entire closed domain. This still defines a genuine convex body with positive interior. The direct inverse-arm, Tonelli, and cap formulas above remain valid for these zero endpoint heights. No assertion from the earlier projective chart that required a positive minimum profile height is imported into this reconstruction.

The reduction applies only when the physical profile already has a horizontal tangent at its source, equivalently when its maximum occurs there. An arbitrary projective tangent chart changes the physical measure. Therefore this note does not convert a general profile to the present class, and it does not prove either the orientation-separated dual inequality or OC. It proves an exact finite-knot replacement for every fixed finite collection of records in this class, including all endpoint and quadratic-moment issues.

# Exact finite-knot replacement of inverse arms

**Exact finite-knot replacement preserving cap records**

For an internal inverse-arm cell, a continuous nonnegative concave nonincreasing arm A with finite inward endpoint slopes and a continuous weight w that is positive in the interior has a concave finite-knot replacement preserving the endpoint values, the required join-slope bounds, and the three records integral wA, integral vwA, and integral wA^2, with at most eight curvature atoms. On a terminal cell, only the initial slope need be finite; a weighted-curvature construction gives at most seven atoms and the same three records, but the completed terminal value may increase. Concatenation over finitely many thresholds yields the stated exact finite-record replacement.

Scope limits: An exact representation/localization result, not the missing scalar cap inequality. The corrected zero-slope coarea is R^m/2 per arm and R^m in total.
